items.description: 社 originally named the local earth god's shrine — the altar raised on a patch of claimed ground for a village's protector spirit. items.meaning_mnemonic: You find the whole character scratched into the mossy step of Grandma Kane's shrine — a cramped grid of hash marks tallying every bell ring. Each mark is a tiny <radical>cross</radical>. Someone crouches there muttering <radical>words</radical> under their breath, counting the same thing for weeks, working out exactly when the shrine sits empty. That obsessive tally is the <kanji>plot</kanji> laid bare.
items.reading_mnemonic: The one holding the chalk turns out to be a cat calling herself <reading>Kay</reading>, perched on the shrine's enormous bell, muttering <reading>けい</reading>, <reading>けい</reading> under her breath as she recounts the marks. She never says another word, just keeps tallying.
items.description: 計 usually means measure, plan, or total in real vocabulary, not a scheme in the dramatic sense this mnemonic uses. Treat the plot here as the calculating, tallying edge of that broader meaning, not a literal conspiracy.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝時計を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I look at the clock every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]時計[とけい]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 私たちは将来計画を考えます。
example_sentences.english: We think about our future plan.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]たちは将[しょう]来[らい]計[けい]画[かく]を考[かんが]えます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼の計画はいいです。
example_sentences.english: His plan is good.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]の計[けい]画[かく]はいいです。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the whole character as a battered <radical>bamboo</radical> abacus, a <radical>chevron</radical> brand burned into its frame, dragged onto the bleachers at Sei's school. The gym teacher's <radical>two hand</radical>s jab at the beads between whistle blasts, one <radical>eye</radical> tracking each row as it clicks past. One bead skitters loose across the bottom wire while she adds up relay times before the runners even finish. That frantic bead-counting is what it means to <kanji>calculate</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The gym teacher's whistle is shaped like a tiny <reading>sun</reading>, and every time a bead clacks into place, it flashes and squeaks <reading>さん</reading>. By the third relay, the whole bleachers are chanting さん along with it.

example_sentences.japanese: 予算はいくらですか。
example_sentences.english: How much is the budget?
example_sentences.furigana: 予[よ]算[さん]はいくらですか。

example_sentences.japanese: この旅行の予算を考えましょう。
example_sentences.english: Let's think about the budget for this trip.
example_sentences.furigana: この旅[りょ]行[こう]の予[よ]算[さん]を考[かんが]えましょう。

example_sentences.japanese: 予算が小さいですが、いいレストランを選びました。
example_sentences.english: The budget was small, but we chose a good restaurant.
example_sentences.furigana: 予[よ]算[さん]が小[ちい]さいですが、いいレストランを選[えら]びました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Late at Koichi's konbini, the beeping till stops mid-scan. The security monitor shows one <radical>person</radical> folded like origami into the walk-in fridge — a <radical>wide box</radical> of steel. Knees to chest, he's framed exactly by its edges. Not one elbow strays past the frame; every part of him is tucked precisely <kanji>inside</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi flings the fridge door open and the man just shivers, chin on his knees, repeating one flat syllable: <reading>ない</reading>. It's the same sound the staff now call him by, <reading>Nye</reading> — the third time this month he's pulled the same fridge stunt.

example_sentences.japanese: これは駅の案内です。
example_sentences.english: This is the station's information desk.
example_sentences.furigana: これは駅[えき]の案[あん]内[ない]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達が新しい店を案内してくれました。
example_sentences.english: My friend showed me around a new shop.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]が新[あたら]しい店[みせ]を案[あん]内[ない]してくれました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅員が図書館まで案内してくれました。
example_sentences.english: The station staff guided me to the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]員[いん]が図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]まで案[あん]内[ない]してくれました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 海 as <radical>water</radical> waves stacked ridge after ridge in a <radical>chevron</radical> pattern, dark and endless. Each one folds over the last until the horizon disappears under them. Somewhere below, a whale <radical>mother</radical> and her calf ride the swell, unbothered. No shore survives that many rows of water — only the <kanji>sea</kanji> does.
items.reading_mnemonic: A diver named Kai plunges past ridge after ridge, lungs burning, and surfaces gasping a ragged <reading>かい</reading>, like shouting <reading>Kai</reading> into the wind, before another wave folds over him.

example_sentences.japanese: 夏に海で泳ぎます。
example_sentences.english: I swim in the sea in summer.
example_sentences.furigana: 夏[なつ]に海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぎます。

example_sentences.japanese: 海岸まで歩きました。
example_sentences.english: I walked to the coast.
example_sentences.furigana: 海[かい]岸[がん]まで歩[ある]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 海はとてもきれいでした。
example_sentences.english: The sea was very beautiful.
example_sentences.furigana: 海[うみ]はとてもきれいでした。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 首 as a face staring straight at you: two tufts of hair on top, one wide unblinking eye below. It's an owl whose head has <radical>split</radical> around backward on its <radical>neck</radical> to watch you from behind its own back, eye locked on yours. That impossible backward swivel is exactly the <kanji>neck</kanji> the character draws.
items.reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, a hiker spots the swiveled owl and yells <reading>Shoo</reading> to scare it off. The owl doesn't budge — it just hisses <reading>しゅ</reading> back through its beak, head still turned the wrong way round. Every hiker who passes gets the same hiss, same stare, same unmoving neck.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の首は長いです。
example_sentences.english: My neck is long.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の首[くび]は長[なが]いです。

example_sentences.japanese: 猫の首は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: The cat's neck is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 猫[ねこ]の首[くび]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.japanese: あの町は首都です。
example_sentences.english: That town is the capital.
example_sentences.furigana: あの町[まち]は首[しゅ]都[と]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 活 as one scene: fizzing <radical>water</radical> <radical>slide</radical>s sideways above a shape jerking back to life below. A commuter has fainted onto the floor of Koichi's konbini, and the clerk empties an energy drink straight into his open <radical>mouth</radical>. His <radical>tongue</radical> recoils at the fizz, and he sits bolt upright mid-gasp, tapping his foot before his eyes open. That fizzing jolt is <kanji>lively</kanji>: revived, helped back onto his feet.
items.reading_mnemonic: The commuter jolts upright and sneezes so hard he headbutts the shelf — a violent <reading>ka-choo</reading> that comes out sounding exactly like <reading>かつ</reading>, onigiri raining down around him. Koichi just restocks the shelf and waits for the next customer to keel over the same way.

example_sentences.japanese: 私の生活はとても忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: My life is very busy.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の生[せい]活[かつ]はとても忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 日本での生活は楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: Life in Japan is fun.
example_sentences.furigana: 日本[にほん]での生[せい]活[かつ]は楽[たの]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日の生活は簡単ではありません。
example_sentences.english: Everyday life isn't simple.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]の生[せい]活[かつ]は簡[かん]単[たん]ではありません。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The kernel stays mid-explosion, husks flung up and down like it never stopped detonating. It scatters across the granary floor until every corner is buried in it. Sweeping the mess into a sack, you finally have a heap of dusty, threshed <radical>rice</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A backpacker named <reading>Bay</reading> wanders into the granary and scoops up a handful of the scattered grain. He tastes it raw, eyes wide, and moans a long <reading>べい</reading>, like it's the best thing he's eaten all trip.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A city planner unveils a scale model of the new capital. A stone <radical>lid</radical> caps the tower like a roof, pressed onto a gaping stone <radical>mouth</radical> propped open as the gate. The whole model sits on a base so <radical>small</radical> she pinches it between two fingers. Lid, gate, tiny base: a capital in miniature.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the ceremony, a boy named <reading>Kyo</reading> knocks the whole miniature capital off the table. It shatters on the floor, and all he can do is groan <reading>きょう</reading>, one long syllable of dread, as the tiny lid and gate pieces roll under the desks.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the top of the trail, the frame with its crossed bars turns out to be a vending machine, each compartment stacked with drinks. A hiker feeds it coins and presses a slot, watching gears click behind the divided panel. Something built only to be put to <radical>use</radical> finally earns its keep.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the summit vending machine, a hiker named <reading>Yo</reading> finally gets her drink and lets out a long, relieved yodel: <reading>よう</reading>, echoing off the ridge. The machine rattles once more, empty and satisfied with its work.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>woman</radical> spins mid-dance, one leg swept wide. Her <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags through spilled <radical>rice</radical>, scattering grains loose. Above her a crooked <radical>chevron</radical> flap flips with each sharp <radical>tap</radical> of the coach's cane. By the last flip, the tally is too high to call anything but a number.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back in that gym, the scorekeeper — a woman named <reading>Sue</reading> — squints at the tally and groans <reading>すう</reading>, dragging the sound out like she dreads the total. The same scattered rice still crunches under her shoes.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, you strike a match for the vending machine's forgotten candle. The two top strokes flare up catching, like a fresh flame; the two splayed legs below are the matchstick still smoking from the strike. That instant, before the fire and everything after it, is the <radical>beginning</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the same trailhead, a hiker named <reading>Gen</reading> singes his thumb relighting that match and yelps <reading>げん</reading>, the exact sound a beginning makes when it starts with a mistake.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank, Grandma Kane unspools a length of <radical>thread</radical> to mark the swimming lane. It is the purest <radical>white</radical> she owns, and the instant it dips into the <radical>water</radical>, the current drags it dead straight downstream. That taut white string cutting across the river is a line.
items.reading_mnemonic: Downstream, lifeguard <reading>Sen</reading> blows her whistle every time that white string drifts off course, barking <reading>せん</reading> until the swimmers straighten back into the lane she marked.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, a <radical>samurai</radical> wedges his armoured shoulders through the gate and roars over the party. Sprawled at his boots is last night's <radical>corpse / body</radical>, still face-down on the mossy steps, undisturbed. That roar shaking the great bell awake is voice.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the shrine steps, star student <reading>Sei</reading> matches the samurai roar for roar, hand shooting up first as always, shouting <reading>せい</reading> loud enough to scatter every cat off the mossy steps.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At school, the gym teacher chalks one flat line onto the <radical>ground</radical>, then a second beside it — <radical>two</radical> lines laid like chopsticks for the new drill. Two coaches grip the yardstick between them, <radical>two hands</radical> holding it dead level, until it tips off the bench and down a gravel <radical>slide</radical>, gone before anyone can grab it. Where it lands, someone rakes <radical>three</radical> claw-mark slashes through the chalk. That rough sketch scratched into the floor is a shape.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the sports field, coach <reading>Kay</reading> stares at the scratched-up chalk sketch and barks <reading>けい</reading> across the field, ordering everyone into position before the shape fades in the rain.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The sleeper sprawls on his notebook, cheek squashed flat, legs dangling off the edge — that limp shape is a <radical>head</radical> gone slack. Beside him a stemmed bowl teeters, heaped with <radical>beans</radical> on crossed legs. He swings an axe to split firewood; the log cracks into <radical>eight</radical>, and one half flies loose, thumping him square on the <radical>head</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the desk, a deskmate spots the bump swelling where the log struck. He winces and mutters <reading>とう</reading>, the same hiss you'd make after stubbing your <reading>toe</reading> on a desk leg.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>lid</radical> is pulled across the sky, and a <radical>person</radical> slips under as the last <radical>evening</radical> drains away. Once the lid is on, nothing more gets in: no sun, no colour. The lid down over the evening: <kanji>night</kanji>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ya is the yakitori man who only opens once the lid is down. The cart comes out of nowhere, the lantern goes up, and he calls one syllable into the dark — 「<reading>や</reading>」 — which is the entire advertisement. If you can hear や, it is night.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail the ground buckles into two long slopes meeting at one high peak. A hiker kicks a stone off the ridge, and it bounces down each slope, funneling into the narrow gap where both sides meet. That draining shape, squeezed into one mouth, is a <radical>valley</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the bottom, the hiker cracks open a can of <reading>coke</reading> and glugs it back with a throaty <reading>こく</reading>, foam sliding down her sleeve while the stone rolls to a stop at her boots.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Beneath the shrine held in <radical>esteem</radical>, its front raised above the mossy steps, a worshipper's <radical>human legs</radical> plant on the flat <radical>ground</radical>. Light pours off the roof in long rays, striking the stone at his feet. That radiance breaking over ground and legs is light.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi arrives to restock the shrine's offering box just as the light rays hit his eyes. He shields his face and grunts <reading>こう</reading>, the same rough sound as a crow's <reading>caw</reading> from the shrine roof.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the riverbank a <radical>drop</radical> slides off a leaf, frozen mid-fall. A fisherman's line snaps into the hook of <radical>nine</radical>, yanking tight around it and reeling it in, coiling around and around until it's squeezed into one tight ball. That coiled sphere, drawn shut on itself, is round.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman reeling in that tight round ball grunts <reading>がん</reading> with every heave, a sound as sharp as a rusty <reading>gun</reading> cocking twice. Neighbors on the riverbank swear they can hear it from their porches.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Toto the door-to-door turtle sets up shop outside Koichi's konbini, hauling a sample <radical>door</radical> off his shell. Its top panel keeps swinging open on its own, scraping against the sill with every gust. He pitches it as a feature: it never latches, so you're never locked out again. Nobody wants that.
items.reading_mnemonic: Outside that same konbini, Toto scrapes his shell along the loose sill trying to force a sale, and each scrape knocks out the same hollow sound: <reading>coh</reading>, <reading>こ</reading>. Shoppers wince every time but can't stop hearing it after they've left. Toto just shrugs it off as free advertising.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> steps onto the thawed <radical>ground</radical>. Boots sink into mud after a whole winter shut indoors. They plant <radical>two</radical> chopsticks upright in the dirt like a garden marker. Then they fling their arms out wide, as <radical>big</radical> as the season deserves. Behind them the sun climbs the window glass to open a new <radical>day</radical>. The whole thawed yard smells like springtime.
items.reading_mnemonic: A groundhog named <reading>Shun</reading> pokes up from his burrow the moment the yard warms, shouts <reading>しゅん</reading>, and dives straight back down out of pure habit. He shuns the cold on principle, but there isn't any today — the mud outside smells exactly like the springtime the person just stepped into.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A groundskeeper spreads a huge hanging <radical>clothing</radical> over the flowerbeds like a tent roof, then rams a signpost <radical>earth</radical> marker into the dirt to claim the plot. He rolls in a stone fountain shaped like a gaping <radical>mouth</radical>, water dribbling down its chin. Tent, staked earth, dribbling fountain: a park.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the new park, gardener <reading>Enji</reading> trips over the fountain's hose and face-plants into the flowerbed. Muffled through a mouthful of dirt, all that comes out is a long <reading>えん</reading>, and the shirt-roof tent collapses on top of him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> droops so low under its own ripe weight that it finally topples into the <radical>fire</radical> crackling beside the field, sparks jumping off both sides as it catches. Farmers burn what's left of the cut stalks every year, before the frost comes. The smell of burnt grain drifting over bare fields is autumn's real signature.
items.reading_mnemonic: A scarecrow standing in the smoking field flaps its sleeves at circling crows and yells <reading>shoo</reading>, <reading>しゅう</reading>, over and over until they scatter. Smoke from the burning stalks stings its painted eyes, but it keeps shouting anyway — the last of the grain only survives if somebody protects it.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Stand on the baked <radical>ground</radical>, cracked and shimmering with heat. Someone points at their own nose — <radical>self</radical>, who, me, out in this? — then a <radical>trailing foot</radical> drags behind, sole gummed to melting asphalt, peeling free each step. That exhausted shuffle across scorched ground is summer.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, sags on a power line above that same baked ground. Too hot even for him, he cracks his beak and a weak puff of flame escapes with a scorched <reading>か</reading>. That tired flame-cough is how you remember summer's reading, <reading>か</reading>.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A hiker plants his <radical>stand</radical> at the edge of a <radical>cliff</radical>. A pot <radical>lid</radical> sits clamped on his head like a hat. <radical>Three</radical> claw marks rake down the rock beside him. Below, someone's <radical>head</radical> lies pressed flat into a notebook page, fast asleep. Stance, hat, scratches, sleeping head — that is the whole face you'd recognize from across the room.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back on the cliff edge, a photographer named <reading>Gan</reading> leans in too close for the shot and slips on loose gravel. He yelps a sharp <reading>がん</reading> as he grabs the rock ledge, dangling right below the sleepy head on the page.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A dockhand swings his axe and splits a log in two, the halves falling apart into a perfect <radical>eight</radical>. He wedges both pieces into the curved hull of a <radical>boat</radical>, then bolts a hatch that gapes open like a yawning <radical>mouth</radical> to swallow the cargo. Split logs, a hull, a gaping hatch: a ship.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the dock, the sailor <reading>Sen</reading> hears the hatch slam onto his thumb and hisses a long <reading>せん</reading> through his teeth, hopping on one foot as the boat rocks against the pier.

items.meaning_mnemonic: The panicking duck yanks again, and a second matching pair of <radical>feathers</radical> pops loose, drifting down to land tip to tip on the pond, mirrored just like the first pair. A fisherman nearby mistakes the twin shapes for a floating insect and casts his line right between them. He reels in nothing but two soaked, stuck-together feathers.
items.reading_mnemonic: The fisherman stares at his soggy catch and groans <reading>ooh</reading>, <reading>う</reading>, disgusted at wasting good bait on nothing but down. He flings the pair back toward the water, where the duck has already forgotten the whole ordeal and gone back to preening at the pond's edge.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A carpenter drags his <radical>angle</radical> gauge to every crooked joint on a lopsided birdhouse. Its sharp peak snags each corner, degree marks climbing the arm as he reads them off. No two corners match, thirty degrees here, ninety there. The birdhouse leans forever, built from nothing but mismatched <radical>angles</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the workshop, the carpenter's uncle, always in a <reading>khaki</reading> jacket, grabs the gauge to fix the leaning birdhouse himself. He measures one corner, grunts <reading>かく</reading>, and nails it anyway, angle be damned. It still leans, but now it leans in his signature khaki style.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A monk drives a wooden <radical>earth</radical> signpost into the temple grounds to mark the boundary. Then he unrolls his <radical>inch</radical> ruler to pace out the plot, tick by stubborn tick. He measures a garden that stretches for what feels like a mile, one thumb-width at a time. By sundown the stakes ring a plot of soil big enough to become a Buddhist temple.
items.reading_mnemonic: The old groundskeeper everyone calls <reading>Jee</reading>, nobody remembers his real name, is the one who planted the signpost and paced out the whole plot with the inch ruler. Visitors greet him with a friendly <reading>じ</reading> before they even reach the gate. He's older than the temple itself now.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> strides into the silk shed just as a <radical>cocoon</radical> finishes sealing itself shut on the shelf. She pulls out <radical>two</radical> long threads at once and works them across a stretched canvas, looping and crossing until a scene appears in the <radical>thread</radical>. Step back, and the tangle resolves into a picture.
items.reading_mnemonic: The embroiderer everyone calls <reading>Kai</reading> signs every finished piece with his initial stitched in the corner: a tiny looped <reading>かい</reading>. Collectors say you can spot his work from across the room, that little loop of thread is his signature every time.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A stray cat creeps up to the butcher's wooden frame, staring through the gap at two slabs of <radical>meat</radical> hanging inside on their hooks. It leaps at the window and rattles the frame, but the hooks hold fast and the slabs just swing. Peer through that same frame, and all you'll ever see hanging there is <radical>meat</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The butcher, whose name tag just says <reading>Nick</reading>, finally chases the cat off with a broom, growling <reading>にく</reading> at it like a curse word. He rehangs the swinging slabs and locks the frame before the cat tries its luck again.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Koichi's konbini the door beeps. A hunched shape stumbles in, head ducked like a pigeon's tucked wing. It lands stiff on the onigiri shelf. Underneath, four skinny stick legs splay out and clatter against the tile like a badly tuned xylophone. The clerk just sighs: it's a <radical>bird</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Everyone at the konbini calls the night clerk <reading>Chow</reading>. He barks <reading>ちょう</reading> at the bird every single night, like he's calling a stray in for dinner. It never once listens.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>drop</radical> hangs frozen mid-fall off a fence post, never landing. Below it, a <radical>trailing foot</radical> scrapes a groove through crusted snow, the boot frozen stiff at the ankle. Between the frozen drop above and the frozen foot below, the whole scene has locked solid — that stillness is winter.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at that fence, a shivering dog named Toby paws at his own frozen <reading>toe</reading> and yelps <reading>とう</reading>, breath crystallizing mid-air just like the drop dangling above him.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Halfway up the mountain trail the steep path suddenly flattens into a clearing. Rows of square rice paddies stack neatly on a thick slab of packed earth. The whole grid sits there through every season without shifting. Hikers stop, catch their breath, and realize they've stumbled straight into a <radical>village</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The village elder who waves hikers toward the paddies goes by <reading>Lee</reading>. Every exhausted hiker calls back a grateful <reading>り</reading> as thanks. That's as much of his name as anyone manages out of breath. He just nods toward the shade.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine the <radical>rain</radical> behind the window freezes mid-fall. Its dashes hang stiff in the glass. Someone drags out the <radical>broom</radical>. Its three bristly prongs sweep the frozen drops into pale drifts over the mossy steps. Even the shrine cats won't leave the bell: it's snow.
items.reading_mnemonic: The groundskeeper everyone calls <reading>Set</reading> mutters <reading>せつ</reading> under his breath every time he has to shovel the steps again. By dawn the drifts are back, deeper than before, and so is his sigh.

items.meaning_mnemonic: On the mountain trail, the vending machine's fan kicks up a strand shed by a passing dog. It hangs in the wind: a flat line at the scalp, hooking into a curl, flicking to a sharp point. It lands stuck to a hiker's sweaty arm, twisting there. That stray curling wisp is <radical>fur</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the vending machine, a hiker named <reading>Moe</reading> picks the stray wisp off his sweaty arm for the third time this climb.
